chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man from us who buys from the Sultan from the camels of charity and the sheep of charity, while he knows that they take from the people more than the right which is obligatory upon them. He said, so he said: 'The camels and sheep are no different than the wheat and the barley and other than that; there is no problem with it until you recognize the prohibited [part] with your own eye.'

It was said to him: 'So what do you think regarding a charity collector who comes to us and takes the charities of our sheep, so we say to him, 'Sell them to us,' and he sells them to us. So what do you think regarding buying them from him?' He said: 'If he has taken them and segregated them, then there is no problem.'

It was said to him: 'So what do you think regarding the wheat and the barley? The apportioner comes to us, so he apportions our share and takes his share and segregates it with a measure. So what do you think regarding buying that foodstuff from him?' He said: 'If he had taken possession of it with a measure, and you were present during that measurement, then there is no problem with buying it from him without measuring it.'
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to buy Zakat goods from the government if they have over-collected from the people?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) establishes that purchasing Zakat assets from the Sultan or collectors is permissible even if they have usurped excess amounts, provided the specific goods have been segregated and taken into their possession (qabd). For grain, the transaction is valid if the buyer witnessed the initial measurement, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the ruler's possession validates the asset despite potential irregularities in collection. This ruling underscores the distinction between the illegitimacy of the exaction and the validity of the subsequent sale of the physical goods.
